1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6.name: French Defence: St. George Defence
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6.background: The name is borrowed from the St. George Defence, 1.e4 a6, named after England's patron saint, which reaches this position with 2.d4 e6. Its first known game is a simultaneous one in which the English amateur J. Baker beat Wilhelm Steinitz on 11 December 1868.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre and guards d4 and e5, keeping the pawn centre flexible instead of committing the c-pawn. It prepares the bishop on d3 and castling, and leaves Black to show whether the queenside advance is really worth the loosening.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4.strategy: Builds a broad three-pawn centre at once and prepares to punish the queenside advance that Black's last move invites: after ...b5 White takes, and the recaptured pawn on b5 stands loose. The price is that the centre is built before any piece is out, so the pawns need support.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4.name: French Defence: St. George Defence, Three Pawn Attack

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5.strategy: A gambit: Black strikes at the c4 pawn and, if White takes, recaptures so as to open the a-file, but the pawn on b5 is then loose and the bishop can win it. An open file and quick development are real but modest compensation, so this is an offbeat try, not a solid choice.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5.strategy: The point of the whole set-up: Black grabs queenside space, takes the a4 and c4 squares from White's pieces and prepares to develop the bishop on the long diagonal against e4. It loosens the queenside, but White cannot easily attack it, since a knight on c3 would meet ...b4.
